title: readonly, Readonly<T>, and immutability flags
hook: The readonly keyword tells TypeScript — and your teammates — that a property or array should not be mutated after creation. It is a compile-time promise: JavaScript still allows mutation unless you copy defensively.

blocks.text: **readonly** marks properties, array types, and tuple elements as not assignable after initialization. The utility type **`Readonly<T>`** shallowly freezes every property on an object type. **`readonly` arrays** (`readonly string[]` or `ReadonlyArray<string>`) disallow `push`, `pop`, and index assignment. Immutability in TypeScript is **enforced at compile time only** — at run time the object is a normal mutable JavaScript object. C# offers stronger guarantees with `init` accessors and immutable collections, but `readonly` in TypeScript is still invaluable for React props, reducer state, and public API contracts.

entries.plainDefinition: A property modifier preventing reassignment after the object is constructed. Does not make nested objects deeply immutable.
Maps every property of T to readonly. Shallow — nested objects remain mutable unless separately wrapped.
Only the top-level properties are readonly. Nested objects can still be mutated unless typed readonly recursively.
entries.example: `Readonly<{ inner: { x: number } }>` — `inner.x` can still change.

blocks.text: React and Angular benefit from readonly props and inputs — accidental mutation causes subtle re-render bugs. Reducers should treat state as immutable: return new objects instead of mutating. Readonly types document intent better than comments. Assignability rules favor readonly consumers — you can pass a mutable array to a `readonly string[]` parameter, but not the reverse (see assignability topic).

blocks.title: Compile-time only
blocks.body: `readonly` emits nothing to JavaScript. Use `Object.freeze` for shallow run-time protection, or copy-on-write patterns for real immutability. Deep immutability needs recursive types or libraries like Immer.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: readonly on properties
items.body: Interface or class field: `readonly createdAt: Date` — assignable in constructor or initializer only.

items.title: readonly arrays
items.body: `readonly number[]` removes mutating methods from the type checker.

items.title: Readonly<T> utility
items.body: Wrap existing types: `type ConfigRO = Readonly<Config>` for function parameters.

items.title: as const for literals
items.body: Freezes literal values and makes tuples readonly — pairs with widening topic.

snippet.label: readonly properties on interface
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–5: `readonly` on `id` and `timestamp` — set once at creation. Line 14: non-readonly `message` remains mutable. Class constructors can assign readonly fields during construction.

snippet.label: readonly arrays and Readonly<T>
snippet.explanation: Line 1: readonly parameter accepts mutable arrays at call site. Line 2: mutating methods are a compile error. Lines 6–8: `Readonly<Point>` prevents reassigning `x`/`y` on the parameter. Line 11: covariance — mutable source, readonly target.

snippet.label: as const readonly tuple
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `as const` makes the array a readonly tuple of literals. Line 4: indexing yields a union of directions, not `string`. Immutability and literal preservation combine.

snippet.label: Shallow readonly trap — nested mutation still allowed
snippet.explanation: Line 5: cannot replace the `user` reference. Line 6: nested `name` is still mutable — classic shallow readonly gotcha. Production code uses Immer or deep mapped types for true nested immutability.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming readonly means deep immutability. Expecting run-time protection without Object.freeze or copy patterns. Trying to pass `readonly T[]` where `T[]` is required — reverse assignability fails.

blocks.text: `Readonly<T>` is shallow; `ReadonlyDeep` patterns use recursive conditional mapped types (module 12). **Mutable vs immutable variance** affects function parameters and React `useState` setters. `as const` produces `readonly` deeply on literals but not arbitrary objects. For public SDK types, export `Readonly<Config>` from factories to prevent consumer mutation. C# `record` with `with` expressions provides value-copy semantics TypeScript lacks natively.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Claiming readonly enforces run-time immutability. Not knowing shallow vs deep. Reversing readonly assignability rules. Unable to contrast with C# init-only setters.

interviewTakeaways: readonly is compile-time only — JavaScript objects stay mutable at runtime.
Readonly<T> is shallow — nested properties need separate readonly typing.
Mutable arrays assign to readonly arrays, not vice versa.
as const produces readonly literal tuples — pairs with union exhaustiveness.
60s: readonly blocks reassignment in the type checker. Shallow by default. Use Immer or deep types for nested safety. C# init/records are stronger at runtime semantics.
commonPitfalls: Expecting deep immutability from Readonly<T> alone.
Passing readonly array to a function expecting mutable T[].
Strong answer: 'Compile-time flag. Shallow unless recursive. Covariant to readonly. Pair with as const for literals.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: `Object.freeze` provides shallow run-time immutability. TypeScript readonly is compile-time only and does not call freeze.
C# `init` accessors and `ImmutableList<T>` enforce stronger contracts. TypeScript relies on discipline plus optional libraries.
